recipes.title: Summer's Vegetable Soup with Wild Greens
recipes.source_note: The Sioux Chef's Indigenous Kitchen, page 65
recipes.description: As summer vegetables start to ripen, we like to make a big batch of this simple soup. It's delicious warm, at room temperature, or chilled.

ingredients.item: wild onion or large shallot, chopped
small summer squash, cut into 1-inch chunks
chopped wild greens such as watercress, purslane, or sorrel

instructions.text: Film a soup pot with the oil and set over medium heat. Sauté the onion until tender, about 3 to 5 minutes.
Add the squash and corn and continue cooking, stirring often, until the squash is tender, about 5 to 7 minutes.
Add the stock and bring to a simmer.
Stir in the greens and mint and cook just until the greens are wilted.
Season with salt to taste.

recipes.title: Missouri River Pozole
recipes.source_note: The Sioux Chef's Indigenous Kitchen, page 66
recipes.description: This hearty soup is our take on the traditional Mexican pozole. Depending on the season, we flavor it with wild greens, mushrooms, or smoked fish.

ingredients.item: wild onion or large shallot, chopped

instructions.text: Film a soup pot with the oil and set over medium heat. Sauté the onion until tender, about 3 to 5 minutes.
Add the hominy, beans, and stock and bring to a simmer.
Stir in the sage and cook for about 10 minutes.
Season with the smoked salt and juniper.
Serve garnished with the radishes and wild greens.

recipes.title: Hearty Mushroom, Sweet Potato, and Bean Soup
recipes.native_name: Čhaŋnákpa na Bló Skúya na Omníča Waháŋpi
recipes.source_note: The Sioux Chef's Indigenous Kitchen, page 67
recipes.description: This warming, earthy soup is perfect for cool autumn evenings. It's hearty enough to serve as a main course.

ingredients.item: wild onion or large shallot, chopped
medium sweet potato, peeled and cut into 1-inch chunks

instructions.text: Film a soup pot with the oil and set over medium heat. Sauté the onion until tender, about 3 to 5 minutes.
Add the mushrooms and continue cooking until they release their liquid, about 5 minutes.
Add the sweet potato, beans, and stock and bring to a simmer.
Cook until the sweet potato is tender, about 20 to 25 minutes.
Stir in the sage and season with salt and juniper.

recipes.title: Fish Head and Wild Rice Soup
recipes.source_note: The Sioux Chef's Indigenous Kitchen, page 69
recipes.description: This soup is a celebration of nose-to-tail cooking. The fish head adds incredible depth of flavor to the broth.

ingredients.item: large fish head from walleye, whitefish, or other freshwater fish
wild onion or large shallot, chopped

instructions.text: Put the fish head and water into a large pot and bring to a boil. Reduce the heat and simmer until the broth is flavorful, about 30 to 40 minutes.
Remove the fish head and pick off any meat, discarding the bones. Return the meat to the pot.
Add the onion, wild rice, and sage and simmer for 10 minutes.
Stir in the greens and cook just until wilted.
Season with salt to taste.

recipes.title: White Bean and Winter Squash Soup
recipes.source_note: The Sioux Chef's Indigenous Kitchen, page 70
recipes.description: This creamy, comforting soup is perfect for cold winter days. The sweetness of the squash balances beautifully with the earthy beans.

ingredients.item: wild onion or large shallot, chopped
small winter squash, peeled, seeded, and cut into 1-inch chunks

Puree about half of the soup in a blender and return to the pot.
Stir in the sage and maple syrup and season with salt.

recipes.title: Hunter's Stew
recipes.source_note: The Sioux Chef's Indigenous Kitchen, page 126
recipes.description: Bear remains a traditional Native food, especially in the Northern Heartland, where these animals are abundant. They're known to raid summer cabins and park dumpsters, and to snatch small pets. Hunting bear for food is one of the best ways to control the expanding population. Moose, elk, and antelope are also great choices for this recipe because the slow cooking helps to turn the meat tender and flavorful. If these are not available, substitute bison or lamb. Serve it over Corn Cakes, page 51, or Cornmeal Mush, page 59, or with Kneel Down Bread, page 55. Like most hearty stews, it will taste better the day after it's made.

ingredients.item: dried wild mushrooms, such as chanterelles, trumpet, or morels
bear, lamb, or bison, cut into 2-inch cubes
wild onions or 1 large leek, white part, trimmed

instructions.text: Put the dried mushrooms in a small bowl and pour the boiling water over them. Soak about 20 minutes until softened. Drain and reserve the soaking liquid. Chop the mushrooms and set aside.

In a large, heavy pot, heat the sunflower oil over medium-high heat and brown the meat pieces in batches, seasoning with salt and juniper. Be careful not to crowd the pan. Cook each batch about 10 to 15 minutes. Remove the browned meat to a platter.
Reduce the heat and add the onions, mushrooms, oregano, and sumac, and sauté until the onion is soft and the mushrooms release some of their liquid, about 3 to 5 minutes.
Stir in the chopped, reconstituted wild mushrooms and the soaking liquid and the stock, stirring to dislodge any brown bits that stick to the pan.

Return the meat to the pot, bring to a simmer, and cook, partially covered, until the meat is fork tender, about 2 hours. Taste and adjust the seasonings. Remove from the heat and let sit a few minutes before serving.

substitutions.substitute: bison or lamb
moose, elk, or antelope

recipes.title: Venison or Elk Stew with Hominy
recipes.native_name: Tȟáȟča naiŋš Heȟáka na Pašláyapi Waháŋpi
recipes.source_note: The Sioux Chef's Indigenous Kitchen, page 131
recipes.description: Venison shoulder is perfect for this recipe. The meat is lean and the muscles break down to become silky and tender during the slow braise. If you can't find shoulder, use shanks. They'll need to cook a little longer but are equally delicious. This is great served with hominy, over Old-fashioned Cornmeal Mush, page 59, or roasted squash.

ingredients.item: wild onions or small shallots, diced
wild mushrooms (chanterelle, oyster, porcini, or cremini), sliced
Corn Stock, page 170, or vegetable stock

instructions.text: Generously season all sides of the venison with the salt and juniper.
Film a cast-iron pot with the oil and set over high heat. Add the venison and sear well on all sides until golden brown, about 4 minutes per side. Remove the venison and set aside.

Reduce the heat and add the onions and mushrooms to the pot and cook, stirring until they brown, about 3 to 4 minutes. Stir in the flour until dissolved; then stir in the stock, cider, and sage and bring the mixture to a boil.
Reduce the heat to a low simmer. Cover and cook until the meat pulls away easily from the bone, about 1½ to 2 hours. Taste and season with the vinegar and sugar.
Transfer the venison to a cutting board and remove the bone. Slice the meat into chunks and return to the pot. Discard the sprig of sage.
Serve in shallow bowls over wild rice, corn cakes, hominy, or roasted squash.

notes: *If venison is not available, substitute lamb or goat in this recipe.

substitutions.substitute: lamb or goat

recipes.title: Chef Freddie Bitsoie's Corn Broth
recipes.source_note: The Sioux Chef's Indigenous Kitchen, page 193 (Indigenous Partners)
recipes.description: Freddie Bitsoie, executive chef at the renowned Mitsitam Café at the National Museum of the American Indian in Washington, D.C., is one of the most sought-after educators and presenters, with a deep knowledge of art history and anthropology. Freddie shares his passion for Navajo (Diné) foods with wit and panache. His simple, elegant recipes are as inspiring as they are accessible. 'This broth is a workhorse in our kitchen; easy to make and more delicious as it simmers on the back of the stove,' he says. 'To make a hearty soup or stew, add smoked fish or duck. Add soaked hominy or beans for a nutritious meal. It will keep several days in the refrigerator and freezes beautifully.'

instructions.text: Combine all of the ingredients, except for the salt and pepper, in a pot. Bring to a boil, then turn the heat down to a simmer.
Simmer for about 3 hours. Strain the broth and discard the vegetables.
Using a paper towel, strain the broth again for clarity. Pour the broth back into the pot.
Place over medium heat and reduce it by three-fourths. Season with salt and pepper, to taste.
Check the seasoning before serving. Serve warm or hot.

recipes.title: Lobster Broth
recipes.source_note: Damn Good Food by Mitch Omer, page 40

instructions.text: Add chopped lobster shells and butter to a large pot. Cook over medium-high heat, stirring continually, for 11 minutes.
Add wine and chicken broth, and heat to a boil. Reduce heat and simmer, uncovered, until total liquid, minus shells, reduces to 4 1/2 cups.
Strain through a fine mesh sieve, and discard solids.

recipes.title: Fish Fumet
recipes.source_note: Damn Good Food by Mitch Omer, page 45

instructions.text: Heat butter in a heavy-bottomed stock pot or large saucepan over medium-high. Add celery, carrot, onion, and garlic, and toss until onions are translucent, about 5 minutes. Do not brown the vegetables.
Add fish bones, and saute about 3 minutes, until bones are opaque. Add wine, and bring to a boil.
Add water, peppercorns, parsley, bay leaf, clove, and thyme, and return to a boil. Reduce heat immediately, and simmer uncovered 31 to 45 minutes.
Strain fumet through a fine mesh strainer and siphon through a double thickness of cheesecloth. Let cool to room temperature, cover, and refrigerate.

recipes.title: Fish Chowder
recipes.attribution: C. Houston Goudiss and Alberta M. Goudiss
recipes.source_note: Foods That Will Win the War And How to Cook Them (Project Gutenberg #15464, public domain)

instructions.text: The Curry stuffs you use for mollagoo tanney should be very fine.
Take a large stew-pan and mix all the above together, only one onion (sliced), garlic and ginger chopped up fine.
Let these simmer for ten minutes, now strain it through a muslin or gravy strainer.
Now fry the other onion in the dessertspoon of butter in another stew-pan.

When the onions are browned add the mollagoo tanney with a small bay leaf, and skim off the grease, and send to table in a soup tureen as a soup; but this should be used instead of soup, or the first dish for a lunch or breakfast or dinner, but I recommend for dinner in Europe.
Cut lemon should be handed round with the above and plain boiled rice.
Fried red herring wouldn't be a bad accompaniment.
In India the mullagatawny is used generally once a week—say on a Sunday or Wednesday.
